cards.back: Start with a relational database unless you can name an access pattern or scale number that rules it out.
Rows keyed by partition and sorted by a clustering key: huge write volumes and time-ordered data per key, like messages. Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable.
Each column stored together and compressed, for scans and aggregates over a few columns of billions of rows. BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse.
Updates pages in place and reads one page per level; upper levels stay in memory, so a lookup costs one or two disk reads at most.
Appends writes to memory, flushes sorted files and merges them in the background (compaction). Reads may check several files, with Bloom filters skipping most.
Every index is updated on every write and takes disk and memory, so index only what frequent queries filter and sort by.
An index on several columns, like (user_id, created_at), for a query that filters on one column and sorts by another.
Atomic (all or nothing), consistent (constraints hold), isolated (no half-done work seen), durable (committed means on disk).
Synchronous waits for a follower: no loss on failover, slower writes. Async waits only for the leader: fast, but failover can lose the last changes. Semi-sync is the middle ground.
Read your own recent writes from the leader for a few seconds, pin a user's reads to one follower, or wait until the follower reaches the write's log position.
Durability (a disk dies, data survives), availability (promote a follower) and read scale (spread reads over followers).

quiz.q: A user updates their profile, reloads, and sees the old version. What is the likeliest cause?
choices: Replication lag on a read follower
quiz.why: Followers can be seconds behind under load; read your own recent writes from the leader.

quiz.q: 'My recent orders' filters by user_id and sorts by created_at. Which index fits?
quiz.why: A composite index serves the filter and the sort together.

quiz.q: You must move money between two accounts so both writes happen or neither does. What do you use?
quiz.why: Transactions give all-or-nothing writes when two writes must agree.

quiz.q: A workload is a massive stream of writes of time-ordered events per key. Which family suits it best?
choices: Single-node relational database with many indexes
quiz.why: Wide-column stores handle huge write volumes and time-ordered data per partition.

quiz.q: A table has eight indexes and inserts are slow. Why?
choices: Every index is updated on every write
The B-tree has too few levels
quiz.why: Each index adds write cost; drop the ones queries don't use.

quiz.q: Failover must lose no committed writes. Which replication mode do you need?
choices: Synchronous or semi-synchronous to at least one follower
quiz.why: Commit must wait for a follower's confirmation so a promoted follower has every write.

quiz.q: You need sum of amounts per month over billions of rows. Which store fits?
quiz.why: Columnar stores scan and aggregate a few columns of huge tables efficiently.
